macro: Wednesday morning economic data was mixed but the headline story is a notably cool August PCE print, with core coming in at +0.2% month-over-month versus the Street's +0.3% estimate and +3.0% year-over-year versus +3.3% expected. Q2 GDP was revised meaningfully higher to +2.2% annualized from +1.5%, driven by upward revisions to investment, consumer spending, and government spending. However, Adam flags that methodological changes to PCE calculation starting with the August reading had a downward impact on price momentum, meaning markets may discount the softer number if it reflects calculation shifts rather than genuine disinflation. market_outlook: Adam leans cautiously bullish on the back of the cool PCE data, but tempers enthusiasm given methodological changes that may have artificially depressed the reading. The key near-term catalysts are Friday's BLS September jobs report and the October 14th CPI print, which will carry more weight than today's August PCE as investors have largely moved on from August data.
bull_case: Core PCE came in well below expectations at +0.2% month-over-month and +3.0% year-over-year, a dovish surprise that supports the case for the Fed to ease further. The July core PCE was also revised lower from +3.3% to +3.0%, reinforcing a disinflationary trend. Q2 GDP was revised sharply higher to +2.2%, suggesting the economy remains resilient even as inflation cools — a soft landing narrative. ADP jobs rebound to +90K signals the labor market is not falling off a cliff.
bear_case: The market-based PCE, which strips out imputed prices, was relatively hot in August at +0.4% headline and +0.3% core, suggesting underlying price pressures may be stickier than the headline number implies. Methodological changes to PCE calculation starting in August had a downward bias on the print, meaning the softer reading may not reflect genuine disinflation and markets could dismiss it. Personal income growth was significantly weaker than expected at +0.2% versus +0.5% forecast, causing the savings rate to shrink — a potential warning sign for consumer durability. Investors are already looking past August data to the September CPI on October 14th, limiting the bullish shelf life of today's print.
sectors: Construction, manufacturing, education/health services, and leisure/hospitality showed job gains in September per ADP. Financial activities and professional/business services were areas of weakness, shedding jobs in September.

tts_summary: Here's your midday macro read for Wednesday, September 30th. The morning was packed with economic data and the headline number that matters most is the August PCE inflation report. Core PCE came in at plus 0.2 percent month-over-month, well below the Street's plus 0.3 percent estimate. Year-over-year, core PCE printed at plus 3.0 percent versus expectations of plus 3.3 percent. The July reading was also revised lower from plus 3.3 to plus 3.0 percent. On the surface, this is a dovish, bullish development — especially coming right after Fed's Williams spoke on Tuesday. But here's the important caveat: there were methodological changes to how PCE is calculated starting with this August reading, and those changes had a downward mechanical impact on price momentum. So if the softer print is mostly a math story rather than a genuine disinflation story, markets won't give it full credit. And that's exactly what Adam is flagging — investors have largely moved on from August data and are already focused on September prices, which won't hit until the CPI report on October 14th. So today's PCE is a positive, but it has a short shelf life. On the growth side, Q2 GDP was revised sharply higher to plus 2.2 percent annualized, up from the prior estimate of plus 1.5 percent. That reflects upward revisions across investment, consumer spending, and government spending. The soft landing crowd will like that number. The ADP September jobs report came in at plus 90 thousand private sector jobs, slightly above the 75 thousand forecast and a big improvement from August's 36 thousand. Strength came from construction, manufacturing, education and health services, and leisure and hospitality. Weakness showed up in financial activities and professional and business services. One concern worth flagging: personal income was a notable miss at plus 0.2 percent versus the plus 0.5 percent expected, and that caused the savings rate to shrink. That's a yellow flag for the consumer over the medium term. Looking ahead, all eyes now shift to Friday's BLS September jobs report. The current forecast sits at plus 90 thousand total jobs. What the market wants is a soft but not scary number — something in the 50 to 75 thousand range would be ideal because it could bring yield relief without triggering recession fears. A horrible print would be bad. A number too hot could reignite rate pressure. Net-net, today's data leans modestly bullish but the real tests are Friday's payrolls and October 14th's CPI. Stay patient and don't over-trade the PCE reaction.
